opus-5.5.text:
I think software development turned out to be a very lucky first proving ground, and it's worth being honest about why. Code has unusually good properties for an agent: the environment is mostly text, actions are cheap and reversible, and you get fast, fairly objective feedback. You run the tests, the compiler complains, the program crashes or it doesn't. So many of the design patterns we now take for granted, like the plan, act, observe, revise loop, tool calling, keeping a scratchpad or a to-do file, spawning sub-agents for subtasks, grew up in an environment that is very forgiving.

When you move to other long-horizon tasks, say research, data analysis, operations work, or anything involving the physical world or other people, some of those patterns carry over really well and some don't.

What carries over, I think, is the structural idea: the model shouldn't try to hold the entire task in its head. Externalizing state into files, notes, and structured memory, decomposing into subtasks with clear interfaces, and having the agent periodically re-read its own progress, those are general solutions to a general problem, which is that context is finite and attention drifts over long trajectories. Coding agents basically discovered good habits of a careful human engineer, and those habits apply anywhere.

What doesn't carry over as cleanly is verification. In coding, "is this step correct?" often has a cheap answer. In a lot of other domains the feedback is delayed, noisy, or subjective. If an agent is writing a market analysis or running a multi-week experiment, there's no unit test. So I think the real frontier is building verifiers, or learning to act well under weak verification: self-critique, cross-checking with independent sources, having separate agents review each other, and knowing when to stop and ask a human.

The second gap is irreversibility. In a repo you can always git reset. If an agent sends an email, moves money, or changes a production system, you can't. So frameworks for general tasks need a much stronger notion of risk: which actions are safe to explore, which need confirmation, how to sandbox. That's less a model capability question and more an environment and product design question, but it matters a lot.

And then there's a training angle that I care about. A lot of the progress in coding agents came because we could do reinforcement learning against real, checkable outcomes at scale. For other long-horizon tasks, the bottleneck is building environments and reward signals that are rich enough to train on without the model learning to game them. I'd say whoever figures out good, scalable environments for those domains will see the same kind of jump we saw in coding.

So my short answer: the scaffolding generalizes, the feedback loop doesn't automatically. Coding gave us the blueprint, but for each new domain you have to rebuild the part that tells the agent whether it's actually making progress.

r002.rationale: It calls for building scalable training environments and reward signals for other long-horizon domains, including tasks such as multi-week experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think software development turned out to be the ideal training ground for agents, almost by accident, and the reason is verifiability. When a model writes code, you can run the tests, you can compile it, you can check whether the pull request actually closes the issue. That gives you a dense, reliable signal at every step, and that signal is what lets you train an agent to plan, act, observe, and correct itself over hundreds of steps. So the frameworks we built for coding, the tool-use loop, the context management, the ability to decompose a task and recover from errors, those are not really about code. They're about operating in an environment where you can check your own work.

The question for other long-horizon tasks is whether you can construct that same kind of feedback. And I'd split those tasks into two groups. The first group looks a lot like coding once you squint: data analysis, scientific computation, operations work, anything where there's an executable environment and a checkable outcome. There, I think the transfer is fairly direct. The agent architecture carries over almost unchanged, and the main work is building the environment and the verifiers.

The second group is harder: research, writing a long report, negotiating, making a product decision. The horizon is long, but the reward is sparse, delayed, and often subjective. Here I don't think you can just copy the coding framework. What does carry over is the skill the model learned inside the coding loop, which is a kind of discipline: keep a plan, track state, notice when something is off, go back and fix it. We're seeing that discipline generalize even when the task has nothing to do with programming. But to push further, you need to invent proxies for verification. Sometimes that's a model acting as a critic, sometimes it's decomposing the task so that sub-goals become checkable even if the whole isn't.

So my honest view is that the architectures transfer, but the real bottleneck is not the framework. It's the environment. Whoever can build rich, long-horizon environments with trustworthy feedback for a new domain will get agents that work in that domain. Coding happened to come with that environment for free. For everything else, we have to build it ourselves, and that's where most of the effort over the next couple of years is going to go.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tracking state, correcting errors, and managing context, but does not identify reviewing earlier modifications after context compression as a requirement.

r002.rationale: It proposes building rich, long-horizon environments with trustworthy feedback for new domains and explains that this feedback enables training agents to plan and act over many steps.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the design carries over, but the feedback loop is the key difference. In software development, an agent can change code, run tests, inspect an error, and try again. That gives it a fairly concrete way to measure progress. In other long-horizon tasks, you may not have such a clear signal.

The transferable parts are things like breaking a goal into smaller steps, keeping track of what has been done, using tools, and revising the plan when new information arrives. But you can’t assume that a framework that works well for coding will work equally well for research or business workflows. You have to ask: How does the agent know that a step succeeded? How does it detect a mistake before building ten more steps on top of it?

So I would borrow the mechanisms, but redesign the verification around the task. Sometimes that means checking against evidence; sometimes it means getting human feedback at an important decision point. For long-horizon work, the critical capability is not just continuing for a long time. It’s being able to recognize when the trajectory is wrong and recover.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tracking completed steps and revising plans, but does not identify reviewing earlier modifications after context compression.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose training agents on deliberately constructed long-horizon tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think many of the design principles carry over, but the feedback loop matters more than the framework itself. In software development, an agent can make a change, run tests, inspect the result, and try again. The environment gives it relatively concrete evidence of whether it is making progress.

For other long-horizon tasks, I would ask: What is the equivalent of running the tests? How can the agent check intermediate results, recognize a mistake, and recover? Breaking work into smaller steps, using tools, and keeping useful memory are broadly applicable. But if the agent cannot reliably evaluate those steps, a more elaborate workflow can just compound errors.

So I would transfer the mechanisms for managing state and recovering from failures, while adapting the verification process to the task. And where success is ambiguous, the agent needs to bring the human back into the loop at meaningful decision points. The goal is not simply to keep an agent running longer; it is to make sure that additional work continues to produce useful progress.
